newsitem.title: UK: Decision on N.Ireland march due, troops arrive.
newsitem.headline: Decision on N.Ireland march due, troops arrive.

text.p: Authorities in Northern Ireland were likely to decide on Saturday whether to ban or approve one of the most controversial and divisive Protestant parades in the province's troubled seven-decades history.

British troops in armoured personnel carriers converged on the town of Portadown while Britain led mediation efforts to reach a compromise between the Protestant Orange Order and Catholic nationalists bitterly opposed to Sunday's march.

Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam urged the Orange Order to "listen to the voices of reason" in a thinly-veiled message to the brotherhood to reroute the parade and avoid a repeat of the province-wide violence it unleashed last year.

But spokesmen for the order, a religion-based pro-British organisation, showed no sign of heeding her appeal and it has refused all contact with the Catholic residents of Portadown's Garvaghy Road area who say the parade is sectarian intimidation.

There was no indication which way the decision, which can be taken by police chiefs or Mowlam, would go but Protestants and Catholics were united in the fear that it would provoke violence irrespective.
The Garvaghy Road, a Catholic enclave on the edge of a Protestant town, was decked in Irish tricolour flags in a show of defiance against the Orange Order's British traditions.
Residents lined the half mile (two km) straight road and held picnics under rare evening sun on Friday to show their determination not to allow the marchers through.

The Orange Order says the march is a birthright and the road belongs to the British crown, not to those who live beside it. Members argues that a ban on the march would insult their religion, civil rights and British loyalties.
The parade has become a trial of strength between pro- British Protestants and pro-Irish Catholic nationalists whose rival allegiances have split the province since it was created seven decades ago.

In the middle is the new Labour government of Prime Minister Tony Blair which pledged after winning May 1 elections that Northern Ireland's 60 percent Protestant majority and 40 percent Catholic minority would enjoy equal rights.

The dispute is clouding Anglo-Irish efforts to give a new impetus to stalemated Northern Ireland peace talks and persuade Catholic-backed Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas to call a halt to their war against British rule.

The row over the the march, known as Drumcree after the small Protestant church where the Orange Order stops for prayers, erupted last year into days of rioting which shut down towns, roads and the airport and caused millions of pounds (dollars) of damage.

Police at first banned the parade, then bowed to Protestant rioting and let it go ahead, escorting a handful of Orange Order members quickly down the Garvaghy Road amid strict security and abuse from residents.
The reversal of the original decision ignited Catholic anger in turn as youths in the nationalist city of Londonderry lit blazing barricades and showered police with petrol bombs for nights on end.
